title: What 264 Hours Without Sleep Does to Your Brain

strategy.viewer: Curious adults who have pulled an all-nighter and wonder how bad it really gets; clicks for the extreme record and the 'drunk brain' hook.
strategy.hook: Seventeen hours awake is like being drunk; eleven days and your brain starts sleeping while you are awake: a familiar fact against an impossible one.
strategy.promise: What really happens in your brain from hour 0 to hour 264 without sleep, with the real cases (Tripp, Gardner) and the science.
strategy.payoff: A brain that will not sleep starts sleeping in pieces (local sleep, microsleeps) while awake, and without full sleep its cleaning flow (glymphatic) never completes.
strategy.takeaway: Stay awake long enough and your brain starts sleeping without you.

scenes.text: Stay awake seventeen hours, and your brain performs like you are drunk.
Stay awake eleven days, and your brain starts doing something it was never built to do: sleeping while you are awake.
scenes.code:
t=Text("11 DAYS",font_size=72,color=YELLOW).shift(UP*1.2)
u=Text("264 HOURS AWAKE",font_size=48,color=WHITE).shift(DOWN*0.1)
v=Text("the brain starts sleeping anyway",font_size=36,color=RED).shift(DOWN*1.3)
self.play(Write(t),run_time=1.5)
self.play(FadeIn(u),run_time=1.2)
self.play(FadeIn(v),run_time=1.5)

scenes.text: We are going to follow one human brain, hour by hour, past the point where it begs to shut down.
label: HOUR 0
You wake up

scenes.text: Two forces decide when you sleep: the pressure that builds while you are awake, and a body clock that says when night falls.
scenes.code:
title=Text("TWO FORCES DECIDE WHEN YOU SLEEP",font_size=40,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
b1=Rectangle(width=1.6,height=0.1,color=ORANGE,fill_color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=1).move_to(LEFT*2.5+DOWN*2.2,aligned_edge=DOWN)
b2=Rectangle(width=1.6,height=0.1,color=BLUE,fill_color=BLUE,fill_opacity=1).move_to(RIGHT*2.5+DOWN*2.2,aligned_edge=DOWN)
l1=Text("SLEEP PRESSURE",font_size=30,color=ORANGE).move_to(LEFT*2.5+DOWN*2.8)
l2=Text("BODY CLOCK",font_size=30,color=BLUE).move_to(RIGHT*2.5+DOWN*2.8)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(b1),FadeIn(b2),FadeIn(l1),FadeIn(l2),run_time=1.5)
t1=Rectangle(width=1.6,height=4.2,color=ORANGE,fill_color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=1).move_to(LEFT*2.5+DOWN*2.2,aligned_edge=DOWN)
t2=Rectangle(width=1.6,height=2.4,color=BLUE,fill_color=BLUE,fill_opacity=1).move_to(RIGHT*2.5+DOWN*2.2,aligned_edge=DOWN)
self.play(Transform(b1,t1),run_time=4,rate_func=linear)
self.play(Transform(b2,t2),run_time=2)
n1=Text("builds while awake",font_size=28,color=WHITE).move_to(LEFT*2.5+UP*2.4)
n2=Text("says when night falls",font_size=28,color=WHITE).move_to(RIGHT*2.5+UP*0.9)
self.play(FadeIn(n1),FadeIn(n2),run_time=1)

scenes.text: Hour zero. You wake, and a chemical called adenosine starts to build up, one minute of sleep pressure at a time.
At seventeen to nineteen hours awake, performance matches a blood alcohol of about point zero five. At twenty-four hours, about point one.
scenes.code:
title=Text("HOURS AWAKE vs DRUNK",font_size=44,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
ax=Axes(x_range=[0,24,6],y_range=[0,0.1,0.025],x_length=9,y_length=4,axis_config={"color":GREY_B}).shift(DOWN*0.4)
xl=Text("hours awake",font_size=30).next_to(ax,DOWN)
yl=Text("equivalent blood alcohol",font_size=28).next_to(ax,LEFT).rotate(PI/2).shift(RIGHT*0.3)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(ax),FadeIn(xl),FadeIn(yl),run_time=1.5)
g=ax.plot(lambda x:0.0003*x**1.55 if x<17 else 0.05+(x-17)*0.007,x_range=[0,24],color=ORANGE,stroke_width=8)
self.play(Create(g),run_time=3.5)
d1=Dot(ax.c2p(18,0.05+0.007),color=YELLOW,radius=0.14); t1=Text("~0.05 at 17-19 h",font_size=32,color=YELLOW).move_to(UP*1.1+LEFT*2.8)
d2=Dot(ax.c2p(24,0.099),color=RED,radius=0.14); t2=Text("~0.10 at 24 h",font_size=32,color=RED).move_to(UP*2.0+RIGHT*1.2)
self.play(FadeIn(d1),FadeIn(t1),run_time=1)
self.play(FadeIn(d2),FadeIn(t2),run_time=1.2)
scenes.fact: Studies compare impairment, not real alcohol:\Nreaction speed matches a drinker's.

scenes.text: Around hour twenty, reaction times slow and mistakes pile up. Tasks that need steady attention, like watching a dashboard, fall apart first.
Caffeine does not erase that pressure. It blocks the receptors that sense it, so the debt keeps growing in the dark.
That is why drowsy driving kills. Not hours of sleep at the wheel, just seconds, with nobody noticing.
label: HOUR 20+
Slower, edgier, forgetful

scenes.text: A microsleep is the brain's emergency shutdown. Your eyes may stay open, but for a moment nothing is being processed.
scenes.code:
title=Text("MICROSLEEP",font_size=48,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
eye=Ellipse(width=4,height=1.8,color=WHITE,stroke_width=6)
iris=Circle(radius=0.7,color=BLUE_C,fill_color=BLUE_E,fill_opacity=1)
pup=Circle(radius=0.3,color=BLACK,fill_color=BLACK,fill_opacity=1)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(eye),FadeIn(iris),FadeIn(pup),run_time=2)
a=Text("EYES OPEN",font_size=36,color=WHITE).shift(DOWN*2)
self.play(FadeIn(a),run_time=1)
b=Text("BRAIN OFF FOR A MOMENT",font_size=36,color=RED).shift(DOWN*2)
self.play(Transform(a,b),iris.animate.set_fill(GREY_D),pup.animate.set_fill(GREY_D),run_time=2.5)

scenes.text: Hour thirty. You are awake, eyes open, answering questions. But parts of your brain may already be asleep.
In 2011, researchers recorded rats kept awake. Patches of cortex briefly switched off, like sleep, while the animal stayed on its feet.
scenes.code:
title=Text("LOCAL SLEEP",font_size=46,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
cells=VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.7,color=GREY_B,fill_color=ORANGE,fill_opacity=0.9,stroke_width=2).move_to(RIGHT*(i-3.5)*0.8+UP*(1.2-j*0.8)) for j in range(3) for i in range(8)])
sub=Text("an awake brain, tired in patches",font_size=32,color=WHITE).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(cells),run_time=1.5)
self.play(FadeIn(sub),run_time=0.8)
import random
random.seed(4)
for _ in range(4):
    pick=random.sample(range(24),5)
    self.play(*[cells[i].animate.set_fill(GREY_E,opacity=1) for i in pick],run_time=0.7)
    self.wait(0.4)
    self.play(*[cells[i].animate.set_fill(ORANGE,opacity=0.9) for i in pick],run_time=0.5)

scenes.caption: DRIVEN BLIND IN A 10-SECOND MICROSLEEP AT 100 KM/H
scenes.text: Ten seconds of microsleep at a hundred kilometers an hour: almost three hundred meters, driven blind.
In 2017, recordings from single neurons in epilepsy patients showed sleep-like slow waves that coincided with attention lapses.
scenes.code:
title=Text("SLOW WAVES WHILE AWAKE",font_size=44,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
ax=Axes(x_range=[0,12,2],y_range=[-1.5,1.5,1],x_length=11,y_length=3.4,axis_config={"color":GREY_B}).shift(DOWN*0.3)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(ax),run_time=1.2)
fast=ax.plot(lambda x:0.35*np.sin(9*x)+0.2*np.sin(17*x),x_range=[0,5],color=ORANGE,stroke_width=5)
slow=ax.plot(lambda x:1.1*np.sin(2.2*x),x_range=[5,12],color=RED,stroke_width=7)
l1=Text("alert: fast, small waves",font_size=30,color=ORANGE).move_to(UP*1.6+LEFT*3.5)
l2=Text("lapse: slow, big waves",font_size=30,color=RED).move_to(UP*1.6+RIGHT*3)
self.play(Create(fast),FadeIn(l1),run_time=2.5)
self.play(Create(slow),FadeIn(l2),run_time=3)
label: EEG, ILLUSTRATION
Not real patient data
scenes.fact: Nir et al., Nature Medicine, 2017:\Nlocal neuron slowing, attention lapses.

scenes.text: Night-shift workers and exhausted office staff can end up in this zone, which is why sleep scientists treat it as a public safety issue.
label: WHO LIVES HERE
Nights, long calls, long roads

scenes.text: Hour thirty-six. Mood sags, and the brain's alarm center, the amygdala, reacts far more strongly to bad news.
label: HOUR 36
Emotions get louder
scenes.fact: Yoo et al. 2007: amygdala response ~60%\Nstronger after a night without sleep.

scenes.text: Memory takes a hit too. After one night without sleep, a study found about nineteen percent fewer new memories were retained.
Hour forty-eight. Two full days awake, and attention lapses grow longer and more frequent.
Hour seventy-two. Concentration crumbles, speech slows, and the world starts to blur.
label: HOUR 72
The edge of reality

scenes.text: New York, 1959. Disc jockey Peter Tripp sat in a glass booth in Times Square and stayed awake two hundred one hours, raising money for charity.
By the third day, he reportedly saw spiders in his shoes. By the fifth, he thought a doctor was an undertaker come to bury him.
scenes.fact: Accounts of Tripp vary; hallucinations\Nand paranoia are well documented.

scenes.text: Researchers think hallucinations may come from dream-like activity leaking into waking, while the brain's reality filter weakens.
scenes.code:
title=Text("WHERE HALLUCINATIONS MAY COME FROM",font_size=38,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
a=Rectangle(width=3.5,height=3.5,color=BLUE_C,fill_color=BLUE_E,fill_opacity=0.7).shift(LEFT*3)
b=Rectangle(width=3.5,height=0.4,color=RED,fill_color=RED,fill_opacity=0.8).shift(RIGHT*3+DOWN*1.55)
la=Text("REALITY FILTER",font_size=30,color=BLUE_C).next_to(a,DOWN)
lb=Text("DREAM-LIKE ACTIVITY",font_size=30,color=RED).next_to(b,DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(a),FadeIn(b),FadeIn(la),FadeIn(lb),run_time=1.5)
a2=Rectangle(width=3.5,height=0.8,color=BLUE_C,fill_color=BLUE_E,fill_opacity=0.7).move_to(a.get_bottom(),aligned_edge=DOWN)
b2=Rectangle(width=3.5,height=3.5,color=RED,fill_color=RED,fill_opacity=0.8).move_to(b.get_bottom(),aligned_edge=DOWN)
self.play(Transform(a,a2),Transform(b,b2),run_time=4)
t=Text("AWAKE HOURS PASS",font_size=34,color=WHITE).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(t),run_time=1)

scenes.heading: RANDY GARDNER, 1963
scenes.text: Four years later in San Diego, seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner set out to beat that record for a school science project. Eleven days.
Friends tested him constantly. On day four he reportedly mistook a street sign for a person, yet on the last night he beat Dement at pinball.
label: DAY 4 TO DAY 11
Confused, yet still capable
scenes.fact: Dement's 1964 observations of Gardner:\Nlapses, yet flashes of normal function.

scenes.text: Stanford sleep researcher William Dement watched him closely. Even then, Gardner's alertness rose and fell with the clock, better in the morning than at night.
scenes.code:
title=Text("THE BODY CLOCK PUSHES BACK",font_size=40,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
ax=Axes(x_range=[0,11,1],y_range=[0,10,5],x_length=10,y_length=3.8,axis_config={"color":GREY_B}).shift(DOWN*0.4)
xl=Text("days awake",font_size=30).next_to(ax,DOWN)
yl=Text("alertness",font_size=30).next_to(ax,LEFT).rotate(PI/2).shift(RIGHT*0.3)
self.play(FadeIn(title),Create(ax),FadeIn(xl),FadeIn(yl),run_time=1.5)
g=ax.plot(lambda x:7-0.45*x+1.8*np.sin(2*PI*x),x_range=[0,11],color=ORANGE,stroke_width=7)
self.play(Create(g),run_time=5)
t=Text("daily dip and rebound",font_size=34,color=RED).move_to(UP*1.6)
self.play(FadeIn(t),run_time=1)
label: STANFORD, 1964
William Dement

scenes.text: After 264 hours, Gardner slept about fourteen hours, then woke up and was largely back to normal within days.
Please do not try this. Gardner was young, healthy, and watched around the clock, and he still showed slurred speech, paranoia and memory lapses.
Gardner's record was celebrated, but Guinness has since stopped recording sleep-deprivation attempts because of the health risks.
scenes.code:
t=Text("264 HOURS",font_size=72,color=YELLOW).shift(UP*1.2)
u=Text("NO LONGER A RECORD CATEGORY",font_size=40,color=WHITE).shift(DOWN*0.2)
v=Text("health risks",font_size=36,color=RED).shift(DOWN*1.2)
self.play(Write(t),run_time=1.5)
self.play(FadeIn(u),run_time=1.2)
self.play(FadeIn(v),Create(Line(LEFT*3.2+UP*1.2,RIGHT*3.2+UP*1.2,color=RED,stroke_width=8)),run_time=1.5)

scenes.text: Recovery sleep is deep. The brain pays back slow waves first, the slowest and most restoring kind of sleep.
label: SLOW-WAVE SLEEP
Recovery comes first
scenes.fact: Deep sleep rebounds first after sleep loss,\Nbefore lighter stages.

scenes.question: How much does the space between brain cells widen during sleep, in mice?
scenes.text: Quick guess before the last part: how much does the space between brain cells widen during sleep, in mice?
Your brain has no lymph vessels, so it uses another system: fluid flowing through channels around blood vessels.
scenes.code:
title=Text("FLUID IN THE CHANNELS AROUND VESSELS",font_size=36,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
v=Rectangle(width=10,height=0.8,color=RED,fill_color=RED_E,fill_opacity=1).shift(DOWN*0.2)
ch=Rectangle(width=10.6,height=1.6,color=BLUE,stroke_width=5).shift(DOWN*0.2)
l1=Text("BLOOD VESSEL",font_size=28,color=WHITE).move_to(v)
l2=Text("channel of brain fluid",font_size=30,color=BLUE).next_to(ch,DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(v),Create(ch),FadeIn(l1),FadeIn(l2),run_time=2)
dots=VGroup(*[Dot(LEFT*5+RIGHT*i*0.9+UP*(0.55 if i%2 else -0.95),radius=0.1,color=BLUE_C) for i in range(12)])
self.play(FadeIn(dots),run_time=0.8)
self.play(dots.animate.shift(RIGHT*1.2),run_time=3,rate_func=linear)

scenes.text: When you fall asleep, a wake-up chemical, norepinephrine, drops, and cells shrink slightly, opening the gaps between them.
In 2013, Maiken Nedergaard's team found that in sleeping mice, the space between cells grew by about sixty percent, and waste washed out faster.
scenes.code:
title=Text("THE GLYMPHATIC FLUSH",font_size=44,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP)
def cells(gap,col):
    return VGroup(*[Circle(radius=0.55,color=col,fill_color=col,fill_opacity=0.5).move_to(RIGHT*(i-1.5)*(1.1+gap)+UP*(j-0.5)*(1.1+gap)) for i in range(4) for j in range(2)]).shift(DOWN*0.4)
a=cells(0.0,RED_C)
lab=Text("AWAKE: tight spaces, waste lingers",font_size=34,color=RED_C).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(FadeIn(title),FadeIn(a),FadeIn(lab),run_time=1.5)
dots=VGroup(*[Dot(RIGHT*(i-2.5)*0.9+UP*(j-0.5)*0.3+DOWN*0.4,color=YELLOW,radius=0.07) for i in range(6) for j in range(2)])
self.play(FadeIn(dots),run_time=0.8)
b=cells(0.55,BLUE_C)
lab2=Text("ASLEEP: spaces ~60% wider, waste flushed",font_size=34,color=BLUE_C).to_edge(DOWN)
self.play(Transform(a,b),Transform(lab,lab2),dots.animate.shift(RIGHT*6.5),run_time=3.5)

scenes.text: That waste includes beta-amyloid, linked to Alzheimer's disease. In one 2018 study, a single sleepless night raised it by about five percent in some brain regions.
That does not prove one night causes dementia. Long-term sleep loss is a risk factor, not a sentence.
The fix is boring and powerful: seven to nine hours, regular timing, and a short nap can reset the worst microsleeps for a while.
So what happens to a brain that will not sleep? It does not stop. It starts sleeping in pieces while you are awake, and the night-time clean-up it relies on gets cut short.
If this changed how you see tonight, subscribe for the next one. And tell me in the comments: what is the longest you have ever stayed awake?
Seventeen hours without sleep makes you perform about like a driver at point zero five.
Study after study found the same thing: your attention slides with every hour awake.
At twenty-four hours, it is about point one, over the legal limit in many countries.
And caffeine does not fix it. It only hides the signal.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.
In 1963, a seventeen-year-old in San Diego stayed awake for two hundred sixty-four hours, for a school science project.
By the end he had slurred speech, memory lapses and paranoia, and doctors wired him to an EEG.
Then he slept about fourteen hours, and recovered.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.

shorts.title: Your brain cleans itself at night

scenes.text: Your brain has no lymph vessels, yet it washes itself every night.
In sleeping mice, the space between brain cells grows by about sixty percent.
Waste, including amyloid, gets flushed out faster. In one study, a sleepless night raised amyloid by about five percent.
The full story is on the channel. Subscribe for the next one.

titles: What 264 Hours Without Sleep Does to Your Brain
Your Brain After 11 Days Without Sleep
Why Your Brain Starts Sleeping While Awake

youtube.description:
What happens to your brain after 24, 48, 72 hours without sleep, and beyond? From the drunk-like brain to microsleeps, hallucinations, and the clean-up your brain does at night, with the real cases of Peter Tripp (1959) and Randy Gardner (1963).

In this video:
- Awake too long
- The drunk brain
- The brain that naps
- Seeing things
- The night shift

FAQ
How long can a person stay awake? The best-known documented experiment is 264 hours (Gardner, 1963-64); it is dangerous and not recommended.
What is a microsleep? A lapse of a fraction of a second up to about 30 s when the brain briefly sleeps.
Does sleep clean the brain? In mice, the space between cells widens ~60% in sleep and waste clears faster (Xie 2013).

Tell me in the comments: what is your longest time awake?

Sources: Dawson & Reid 1997, Nature 388; Williamson & Feyer 2000, Occup Environ Med; Vyazovskiy et al. 2011, Nature 472; Nir et al. 2017, Nature Medicine 23; Yoo et al. 2007, Current Biology (amygdala) and Nature Neuroscience (memory); Xie et al. 2013, Science 342; Shokri-Kojori et al. 2018, PNAS 115; Gulevich, Dement & Johnson 1966, Arch Gen Psychiatry (Gardner).
